This paper shows that any such spine is topologically equivalent to a surface of genus zero, and as a result, it has a unique point of highest elevation. This property enables us to establish a combinatorial interpretation of the Euler characteristic of the spine. Additionally, we investigate how this property applies to tunnel number and cubic number, and we derive upper bounds for these invariants based on the number of peaks in the spine. This research is a preliminary step towards exploring the relationship between peaks and these invariants. Furthermore, we prove that any right-angled Artin group with a spine that is topologically equivalent to a genus-one surface has a finite index subgroup that contains a copy of the modular group. This result is related to a conjecture about the non-singularity of the moduli space of such groups. This research was inspired by previous work on fundamental groups of surface triangulations and line arrangements.

Since selecting and labeling individual anomalies in normal situations is complex and time-consuming, there's a need for methods that can efficiently label large amounts of normal data to facilitate the development of normal data sets for training.  We've developed an innovative approach that utilizes normal data with annotated positive and negative regions to train a model to make reliable predictions on new, unknown objects.  By leveraging an easy-to-determine benchmark for positive and negative examples, we've established specific criteria that ensure the model's accuracy in distinguishing known objects.  To accomplish this, we've developed a method that can efficiently label large amounts of normal data by determining whether newly discovered objects are similar to those in the initial data set.  Using this approach, we've created two normal data sets for the MS COCO dataset, containing 10,004 and 1,000,014 annotations respectively, and have compared its effectiveness against random labeling methods when combining with anomaly detection models, resulting in our approach outperforming the competition by up to 7.7% in AP scores. Theoretical analysis and experimental results show that utilizing subcarriers can enhance localization accuracy, which depends on the system configuration and physical environment.  The proposed method is robust to varying loading on the WiFi access point, and the associated localization error can be minimized by optimizing a parameter related to signal modulation.  Experimental validation is conducted in an office space and a shopping mall, resulting in accurate indoor localization across multiple tests.  The associated source code is publicly available for further research and development.

While previous studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of instruction through demonstration for task-based learning, they were limited to skilled workers who had prior experience with the tasks. In contrast, our research aims to broaden the scope of this approach by enabling less skilled workers to learn complex tasks performed by others from a video. To achieve this, we developed a unique system that allows users to easily annotate video recordings of themselves performing tasks, which then generates text-based instructions based on visual and movement data. The system utilizes movement analysis to create engaging and effective instructions that mimic the movements of the original performer. In our research, we address challenges such as movement alignment, path encoding, and quality assessment to ensure that instructions are not only engaging but also precise and easy to follow. We tested and validated our approach by having unacquainted participants perform tasks based on video demonstrations created by different annotators. The results showed that our method yields high-quality results with regards to learning outcome, similar performance to baseline methods, and reduces the time and effort required to create video-based demonstrations by half when compared to alternative approaches. Furthermore, we observed a notable improvement in learning speed and a significant reduction in errors when using our approach. Additionally, we found that our system produces consistent results even with repeated use and variations in annotation. In contrast to other methods, our approach enables the creation of demonstrations from video recordings performed by non-expert annotators, which results in notable improvements in learning outcomes, with minimal investment in time and effort by both the annotator and the learner. Overall, our research presents a groundbreaking opportunity for interactive video-based learning experiences that are engaging, effective, and effortless to create and consume. In this work, we introduce the concept of a co-creation interface that enables the generation of high-quality, real-time text and image pairs from video recordings of tasks performed by non-expert annotators, with potential applications in the creation of instructional content, data augmentation, and proxy data generation for few-shot learning scenarios. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in generating diverse and precise annotations, with benefits for both the annotator and the learner, and with costs that are marginal in time and effort. Unfortunately, implementing an exact SPS process is theoretically impossible due to the inevitable occurrence of multi-photon events resulting from the interaction between the coherent state and a parametric down-converting material. Nonetheless, various approximations and SPS models have been proposed, with some claiming the ability to achieve nearly ideal single-photon subtractions using simple linear transformations on the state's symplectic matrix. This paper challenges these claims by demonstrating that these proposed SPS models are fundamentally unstable and cannot maintain the desired subtractions while keeping other properties intact. This instability is shown to cause significant problems, including the permanent loss of subtractions along with other issues, as soon as more than two photons are involved. Consequently, we are left with the conclusion that none of the proposed SPS models are viable for creating reliable multi-photon states necessary for the demonstration of multi-photon quantum information processing. The bi-kink state can be viewed as a state with opposite charges on two distant points in a charged sensor. We show that its non-equilibrium behavior is highly affected by whether a 2-sphere surrounding the state has a temperature or not. At zero temperature, the state evolves back and forth between two identical puffs, while in states with an above-zero temperature, the distance between the puffs decreases as the temperature rises. Additionally, we discovered that a specific mode related to the angle on the boundary of the sensor starts oscillating in states with an above-zero temperature, indicating that the state could be used to study a sensor's thermal response to changes in its boundary conditions. Lastly, we found that both the mode and the distance between the puffs behave differently in states with an above-zero temperature as the sensor's impact on the state is considered, leading to us concluding that the bi-kink state may be useful in studying both a sensor's thermal response to changes in its boundary conditions and how charges behave in both equilibrium and non-equilibrium situations.

However, currently available offline methods only apply to a single task, as they utilize a trajectory-dependent loss function that incorporates past experiences.  To tackle multiple tasks, they would need to retain and process extensive amounts of data, significant amounts of which would be unnecessary as tasks are typically learned over a specific set of observations.  We address this issue by proposing a new multi-task offline reinforcement learning approach.  This approach learns a separate policy for each task, but all policies share a unified encoder that converts observations into internal representations.  By preventing the internal representations from depending on past experiences, we can restrict the loss function to be dependent only on current observations, which significantly simplifies learning multiple tasks.  We further enhance our approach by implementing a communication mechanism between task-specific encoders and the unified encoder.  This communication enables the internal representations to convey relevant information about each task, which allows the approach to handle any combination of tasks.  We evaluate our approach on complex robot manipulation datasets, and the results show that it successfully learns multiple tasks using a static dataset.  Compared to standard multi-task reinforcement learning methods, our approach achieves a substantial speed-up when learning from a dataset, as well as a significant reduction in data requirements when learning from a single trajectory.  Additionally, we introduce a critical observation: that data augmentation can compromise the stability of offline reinforcement learning.  We mitigate this issue by designing an innovative criterion that prunes unnecessary transitions, which enables the approach to handle a wide range of data augmentation settings.  We support our method's benefits with thorough theoretical analysis and experimental evaluations.  When learning from a single trajectory, our approach is equivalent to learning multiple tasks over a specific set of observations, which is the key to its simplicity.  When learning from a dataset, the approach's complexity arises from selectively retaining relevant transitions for each task, which is the key to its efficiency.  We demonstrate the approach's stability across a range of data augmentation settings, and the results show that it successfully learns multiple tasks and outperforms standard multi-task reinforcement learning methods.  Compared to recent multi-task offline methods, our approach learns multiple tasks at a higher frequency and requires less data to achieve convergence. of games characterized by the absence of a global payoff function. Instead, the value of the game is determined by the minimum expected payoff to one of its players across all possible scenarios or states of nature. This type of game theory problem was first explored by John Nash in his work on cooperative games. We investigate two specific types of extended games: those defined by a finite set of state-dependent payoffs and those described by an infinite set of such payoffs. For the former type, we demonstrate that any agreement reached among players will result in a similar outcome, known as an $\epsilon$-efficient solution, where $\epsilon$ represents a small positive variation in expected payoff. However, the concept of $\epsilon$-efficiency may not apply universally to games with an infinite number of states. We also examine two methods used to classify these infinite games: based on whether their value varies continuously with changes to their description, or through the application of a specific ordering system. Finally, we provide examples of both continuous and discrete games with either finite or infinite descriptions. 

  The research presented in this paper was influenced by earlier studies on cooperative games and their connection to topological properties. We aim to build upon existing theories and provide new insights into the theory of extended games. These findings may have implications for the study of cooperative games and their connection to the concept of efficiency. 

  The paper's results can be interpreted as demonstrating the existence of $\epsilon$-efficient solutions in both finite and infinite games. However, this interpretation is contingent upon the understanding that $\epsilon$ represents a very small positive variation in expected payoff.

This study introduces a new detection method called a MDoS traffic-aware cooperative sensing scheme based on cooperative communication techniques, specifically designed to identify MDoS attacks and estimate corresponding traffic amounts. Furthermore, the estimated attack traffic shows a higher degree of accuracy with the proposed system, resulting in an 80% reduction in estimation error when compared to the reference system.  We also explored how different antenna configurations affect system performance and found that increasing the number of antennas leads to a significant improvement in performance, with the proposed system achieving a 90% reduction in false alarm rates and 90% reduction in missed detections when using multi-element antennas.  With these results, we argue that the MDoS traffic-aware cooperative sensing scheme represents a more effective approach to detecting MDoS attacks, especially in scenarios where cooperative communication techniques are employed.  However, further research is needed to address potential time delays associated with cooperative transmission, particularly in real-world applications. Abstract: This paper introduces the concept of weak symmetries in k-algebras, establishing their connection to classical weak symmetries. The paper then explores their independence under k-algebra morphisms, as well as their properties in various algebra types, including Lie and Jordan algebras, and even extends the discussion to Lie superalgebras, revealing implications for the algebra's ideal structure.

This revised model incorporates a hidden sector contributing to both dark matter and dark energy, while avoiding the cosmological modularity issue. We examined the parameter space restrictions imposed by various experimental limits and found suitable solutions. These solutions include a hidden sector with a light singlet dark matter particle, resulting from either direct production or through mediation by a heavy neutrino. Additionally, we discovered that the model can explain the observed dark matter abundance with little relic density, thus preventing overproduction in various scenarios. Furthermore, we found that the model often yields dark energy components much less than 80%, leading to a shift in the cosmic density ratio $\Omega_{DE}/\Omega_{DM}$. This changed ratio may have implications for the relevance of certain astrophysical objects in dark matter research, such as small galaxies and galaxy clusters. We also analyzed the effects of hidden sector particles on neutrino physics and found that in some cases, the model may fail to adequately explain the observed neutrino flux at high energies. Lastly, we found that the model typically results in a shift in the WIMP-nucleon interaction cross-section, which may be confirmed or disputed by ongoing and future experiments. contribution, which involves developing strategies to minimize the impact of
perturbations on system stability. This can be achieved by optimizing an
objective function that reflects the growth of eigenvalues, thus offering a
practical solution for solving some optimal control problems of infinite

We demonstrate that the accuracy of these methods is directly related to the size of a particular parameter, which we term the 'action parameter.' Systems with small action parameters serve as suitable candidates for numerical investigation using these methods, which we propose as a standard for verifying the performance of symplectic integrators. Notably, we find that the classical Hénon-Heiles model does not fit this criterion due to its singular nature, despite being commonly used as a test case. We also introduce a modified variant of this system, which serves as a suitable reference system for evaluating the performance of symplectic integrators. Through our research, we highlight the importance of carefully selecting test systems when assessing the accuracy of symplectic integration methods. Ultimately, our work provides a set of criteria and reference systems that can be used to develop more efficient symplectic integrators for long-term integration of celestial mechanics-type problems. 

  We further investigate the application of generalized leapfrog integration to a widely adopted artificial potential force, which serves as a common challenge in celestial mechanics-type problems. Based on our research, we identify key limitations of this method, which include its inability to maintain symplectic properties and precise conservation of certain parameters when integrating a system with an increasingly large action parameter. To overcome these limitations, we propose a novel modified Hamiltonian leapfrog integration method, which guarantees the preservation of symplectic properties and precise conservation of parameters regardless of the system's action parameter size. Through our comparison of these methods, we establish a set of best practices and reference systems that can be used to develop more efficient symplectic integrators for long-term integration of celestial mechanics-type problems. 

  We also explore the application of our proposed method to integrate the Hénon-Heiles system with a small action parameter, which serves as a challenging test case. Based on our results, we identify key artifacts associated with this system, which include the appearance of a periodic orbit, the migration of a planet in a multi-body system, and the occurrence of a close approach in a real-world astrodynamics scenario. Through our research, we demonstrate that our proposed method exhibits superior performance in detecting these artifacts when compared to standard symplectic integrators. 

  We investigate the action parameter size of a system on the basis of its numerical characteristics, which include convergence patterns, divergence thresholds, and periodic orbit detection times.

of some of the world's most sophisticated neutron and muon experimentation tools. 
SNS scientists rely on the performance of two linear accelerators to effectively 
operate their experiments. Accurate operation of these accelerators is crucial, 
mainly because of the complex nature of neutron protein structure and muon physics. 
To ensure the best possible outcomes, accelerator performance needs to be optimized, 
which is best achieved through precise theoretical predictions of beam properties. 
This paper delves into the details of a newly developed fast, reliable, and user-friendly software platform called AROffLine. 
AROffLine represents the combined efforts of several experienced experts in the field 
of accelerator physics, who have incorporated established but dispersed code components 
into this new program on beam calculation and optimization, specifically designed 
for two linear accelerators. In addition, this program includes a unified dataset 
for beam measurement comparison, which is essential for accurate comparison and 
metric definition across different beam parameters. 
In this paper, we discuss the key elements of the program's architecture, detail the 
implementation of beam calculation and optimization processes, and explain the 
dataset management system. 
We also highlight the program's client-server capabilities, as well as the integration 
of a graphical user interface created using Python's PyQt, which has streamlined user 
interaction. 
Throughout the development process of AROffLine, the program has undergone substantial 
improvements, resulting in enhanced prediction accuracy of up to 5% for key beam properties 
following various injection events. 
A key feature of the program is its ability to predict beam properties with high levels 
of precision when confronted with diverse beam scenarios, including full, half, and empty 
batches, as well as different pulse structures and frequencies. 
In addition, AROffLine has successfully optimized beam performance in real-world 
applications, as presented in this study. 
The program continues to be developed in collaboration with researchers at the Spallation 
Neutron Source, where it is used for beam calibration and optimization. 
This software is now openly accessible, along with the accelerator research dataset, 
through a public repository site. 
The program, along with the dataset, is also presented in a companion paper. 
The AROffLine source code is available for download on GitHub at the provided URL.

While traditional neural networks rely heavily on fixed pre-trained word 
embeddings, they lack a clear method to rotate the embedding matrix. 
In contrast, graph neural networks utilize random initialization for 
node representations and refine them during training. 
However, the random initializations may not adequately capture the 
underlying structure of the data, particularly in domains with clear 
taxonomies, such as datasets with overbid connections between related nodes, 
where the data structure is more likely to be leveraged by rotation operations. 
To address this issue, we devise a new approach called Struc2Vec, 
which generates domain-agnostic node representations by combining random 
initializations with rotation-sensitive structure preserving units. 
Experimental results on multiple datasets from diverse domains show our 
approach outperforms existing methods using fixed pre-trained word embeddings 
like Google's word2vec, particularly in domains with clear taxonomies. 
Struc2Vec also yields competitive performance compared to other graph neural 
networks, while proving our method's rotations are indeed sensitive to 
structure, which is a crucial property for a method aiming to replace random 
initializations with deterministic embeddings.  Finally, we show our 
approach is scalable to large datasets containing millions of nodes and 
thousands of classes, successfully demonstrating its potential to become 
a go-to method for domains with complex structures and clear taxonomies. 
The code for Struc2Vec is available at https://github.com/leowyleo/Struc2Vec.

The study focuses on the impact of counter-flow velocities between 0.1c and 0.5c on the jet's structure. With no pressure equilibrium assumed, the analysis reveals that increasing counter-flow velocities cause the initial hot gas ringdown oscillations to die out more quickly, and lead to the formation of a composite shock wave boundary layer within the jet. The rotation of the jet's vortex ring is inhibited as counter-flow velocities increase, and a secondary shock wave is generated which interacts with the main shock wave, resulting in a wedge-shaped structure. The jet's mixing rate is reduced due to the formation of a boundary layer, but increases again at higher counter-flows when the primary vortex ring forms. The location of the composite boundary layer within the jet determines whether pressure equilibrium occurs, and the shape of the pressure profile is influenced by the formation of shocks within the jet. The results are presented through graphical representations of pressure, temperature, and velocity distributions, as well as detailed descriptions of the jet's behavior across various counter-flow velocities. In addition, essential parameters including ringdown pressures, mixing rates, and pressure profiles are tabulated for both zero and negative pressure equilibria situations. The analysis shows that at higher counter-flows when pressure equilibrium occurs, the pressure reaches half at approximately twice the speed of sound, which is in agreement with analytical estimates made by previous researchers. The study confirms that a counter-current air flow has the potential to enhance the efficiency of reactive sonic jets by reducing the rate of mixing with the surrounding environment, and this effect is more pronounced when there is no pressure equilibrium. The analysis also reveals that pressure equilibrium occurs more quickly at higher counter-flows, and this accelerated process is characterized by a higher speed of sound. The findings related to pressure equilibrium hold significance for the design of sonic jet thrusters that operate in an upper atmosphere or in a vacuum, and involve a counter-current or counter-flow component, as in the case of planetary entry missions, chemical propulsion systems, and pulsed jet thrusters. Based on this observation, we propose a novel strategy for training these networks by leveraging constrained optimization techniques. However, this approach overlooks how rotation curves change within the galaxy and may not accurately capture the relationship between galaxies and halos in a more detailed, higher-resolution analysis. To resolve this issue, we re-examine the galaxy-halo connection using a semi-analytical model where rotation curves are described by a de Falco profile, and then compare the resulting models to observations. By fitting this profile to observations of a simulation's galaxies, we derive a universal relationship between their maximum rotation velocity and stellar mass. Based on this, we demonstrate that the radial profile of galaxies is primarily determined by the mass of the halo in which they reside, but also reveal how this parameterization falls short at higher resolution scales, necessitating a more nuanced understanding of the galaxy-halo connection that takes into account the distinct structures within galaxies. Furthermore, we establish that to accurately reproduce the characteristics of galaxies in observations, the model must incorporate a more intricate interplay between baryons within halos, and account for the diverse ranges of galaxy rotation velocities and their correlation with the masses of the surrounding halos. This more intricate approach is essential for obtaining accurate results at higher resolution scales in simulations of the evolution of the universe. Additionally, we provide explicit equations for the relationship between the maximum rotation velocity of galaxies, their stellar mass, and the radial distance from the center, based on the parameters of the simulation and the model used. This enables further analysis of the galaxy-halo connection and its implications in subsequent epochs of galaxy evolution. ube model is a widely-used theory to describe blood flow resistance in small vessels. It is commonly applied in computational hemodynamics to reduce the need for resolving flow details within the body. Although widely adopted, the traditional tube model has several limitations, particularly its incompatibility with non-Newtonian blood models. This study explores possible implementations of the tube model that address these concerns, offering different alternatives such as fractional volume modeling, power-law blood, and two-region models. We demonstrate the practical applications of these methods by simulating blood flow in large vessels, in conjunction with the RANS-Newtonian tube model, and verify their appropriateness through comparison with a detailed hemodynamic simulation. The results show that the two-region model offers the most accurate representation among the presented approaches, providing a suitable compromise between physical realism and computational efficiency. The proposed methods may facilitate future developments in computational hemodynamics, enabling the use of non-Newtonian blood models in large-scale hemodynamic simulations. The implemented methods are also highly versatile and can be applied in conjunction with other scale models, such as the point-counterpoint method, to study flow resistance in small vessels. The study provides a framework for resolving flow resistance in small vessels while keeping the computational demands of large-scale hemodynamics simulations manageable. The employed methods can be made publicly available upon request, along with the used code and datasets. Nevertheless, the study's key contributions revolve around its conceptual frameworks rather than the developed methods, which are primarily a combination of previously-published works. We experimented with two rotation-based methods,  specifically one that uses a single model to process multiple views,  and one that uses a separate model for each view,  evaluating our approach on the UP3 dataset. This study introduces an innovative approach to assign these elements to the appropriate sections of the patent document.  Initially, a deep content extractor model is trained on labeled sections of a comprehensive patent database to identify the underlying structures and thereby enhance the accuracy of subsequent element identification.  Next, a classification-based approach is employed to determine the elements within each section of the patent document. The experiments conducted on various patent datasets demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed approach in accurately identifying the elements within each section of the patent document. {\large Abstract}
\end{center}

Interfaces between transition-metal oxides are able to exhibit unique physical properties 
resulting from their complex electronic structures. Despite this, understanding their local 
magnetism remains a topic of investigation. We utilize two-component tight-binding models to 
analyze interfaces between nickel oxide and manganite, and reveal their complex electronic 
structures through layer-resolved studies. These studies show that mixing between localized 
and itinerant electrons occurs at the interfaces, and demonstrate how this mixing affects 
the local magnetism by comparing measured and calculated spectra. Additionally, we use 
layer-resolved analysis to investigate intermediate valence state in manganite, and show how 
it is influenced by nickel oxide. These findings provide insight into the local magnetism 
present at transition-metal oxide interfaces, and could be applicable to other systems. 
We propose that two-component models can accurately capture the mixed localized/itinerant 
behavior found at oxide interfaces, and suggest these models could be useful for designing 
functional materials with unusual electronic properties through interface engineering. 
Further, we find Lanthanide 4d and 5d states play a key role in localizing the charge on the 
Manganite side of the interface, which may have implications for spin orbit coupling effects 
in these systems, and provide experimental and theoretical evidence for our findings by 
combining Spectroscopy with TB calculations. 
}

This wobble causes changes in the climate in different regions, but it primarily affects areas near the poles.

These vibrations, or gravitational waves, would have affected the Earth's rotation, possibly altering the planet's magnetic field and causing massive geological events like massive flood basalts and volcanic eruptions.

In the algebraic context, consider a projective variety $X \subset \mathbb{P}^m$ defined by polynomials with coefficients in an algebraically closed field $\mathbf{k}$. The path space of $X$, denoted $\Pi(X)$, can be viewed as a subvariety of the bundle $X \times \mathbb{P}^m$ over the identity point, parameterized by directions in which $X$ can be varied. 

For a non-singular curve $X$, the first homology group of the path space $\Pi(X)$ evaluates the algebraic curve along its singular points, yielding an integer value corresponding to the number of those points. 

Extending this to a surface defined by a single equation, if the equation is non-singular, the path space $\Pi(X)$ is also non-singular, resulting in its Picard group being equivalent to that of the surface itself, denoted $Cl(X)$. 

Furthermore, if the equation has a finite, non-singular point, the Picard group of the path space $\Pi(X)$ will be isomorphic to the Picard group of the surface, combined with an infinite cyclic group, $Cl(X) \oplus \mathbb{Z}$. 

In the differential context, let $X$ represent a non-singular projective variety defined by polynomials with coefficients in the algebraically closed field $\mathbf{k}$. The path space of $X$, denoted $\Pi(X)$, can be viewed as a subvariety of the bundle $X \times \mathbb{P}^m$ over the identity point, parameterized by infinitesimal directions in which $X$ can be varied. 

For a non-singular curve $X$, the first homology group of the path space $\Pi(X)$ evaluates the algebraic curve along its singular points, yielding an integer value corresponding to the number of those points.

This is because current deep learning models, which excel at other image recognition tasks, can become trapped in a viewer-centric viewpoint. To overcome this limitation, we have developed an innovative approach that utilizes self-attention mechanics to break free from the viewer's perspective and extract rotational symmetries from images. By building a model incorporating these mechanisms, we have created a system that can accurately identify the structural patterns in images from various angles. Our approach was applied to the task of categorizing visual patterns based on their spatial relationships, and our results show that our model can do this effectively, even when images are viewed from different angles. To further test the flexibility of our approach, we designed a new dataset called PVIP-50, which contains images from 50 different categories and varied viewing angles. Our model's performance was found to be inconsistent with our designed dataset, however it did perform well on the test set following data augmentation, which included applying projection transformations to training and validation images. Notably, our model's performance was found to decline when images with significant distortions were used, which may be an area for future improvement. of a local minimum for a specified function that incorporates the Kac functional, under specific conditions. This involves establishing the relation between the lower bound of the specific function and the variance of the Gaussian free field, particularly for discrete Gaussian multiplicative chaos generated by fractional Brownian motion. Our proof relies on an inequality that compares the expectation of a product of independent random variables to the expectation of the product of dependent random variables, which in turn enables us to apply an inequality from Lopez-Mendoza and Ray. Additionally, we demonstrate the existence of a local minimum for another function that relates volume processes to the Kac functional, under certain conditions. This result has implications for the asymptotic behavior of certain types of random fractals, such as level sets of the fractional Brownian motion and local extremes of the range of Lévy processes. Our approach involves establishing a connection between these results and the existence of a local minimum for the specified function, which can be shown to occur at a particular disorder parameter value. This, in turn, enables us to conclude the existence of an alternative local minimum for another function, which is utilised in studying the asymptotic behavior of volume processes. Our study also highlights the relevance of new open problems related to the existence of local minima for other functions that relate the Kac functional to specific parameters, which are crucial in understanding the asymptotic behavior of certain types of random fractals. These results are primarily outcome of discussions and joint work with R. Durairaj, K. Kal cik, L. Lopez-Mendez, M. Ni, L. Zambra, and X. Zhang. 

Keywords: Gaussian free field, Kac functional, fractional Brownian motion, Gaussian multiplicative chaos, local minimum, variance bounds, Gaussian vector fields, stochastic analysis, probability theory.

Abstract: This article presents an overview of recent advances in the study of fractional Brownian motion, specifically focusing on results related to the existence of local minima for functions that incorporate the Kac functional and variance bounds. These results have implications for the asymptotic behavior of certain types of random fractals, such as level sets of fractional Brownian motion and local extremes of L\'evy processes. Our study highlights the relevance of new open problems related to the existence of local minima for other functions that relate the Kac functional to specific parameters, which is crucial in understanding the asymptotic behavior of these fractals. These results are primarily outcome of discussions and joint work with several colleagues.

Unfortunately, numerous life-threatening diseases remain untreated due to the limited understanding of the complex structure and function of antibodies.  To overcome this knowledge gap, we conduct an in-depth analysis of the crystal lattice formation process in antibodies, incorporating elements from spin ice and geometrical packing theories.  Our investigation yields a quantitative, thermodynamically derived framework that predicts lattice patterns for antibodies based on their unique characteristics, refining them with the inclusion of charge considerations.  By applying this framework to over 6,000 unique antibodies and multiple antibody subclasses, we identify distinct lattice patterns and charge distributions that can inform researchers about the potential spatial arrangement of antigens and the location of critical regions for antigen-antibody interaction in various diseases.  Furthermore, our study reveals novel insights into the fundamental principles of antibody assembly and antigen recognition, while also providing a method for predicting lattice structures that can guide experimental research, such as crystallography and biophysical protein design.  To complement these findings, we develop an open-source software platform called CrystalAb that enables users to simulate and visualize the crystal structures of antibodies within lattice assemblies.  By leveraging this computational tool, we explore the possibility of designing antibody crystals with specific lattice patterns and charge distributions that mimic those found in natural antibodies, thereby potentially enhancing their effectiveness in treating diseases.  By advancing our understanding of the complex structure and function of antibodies, this research has the potential to influence multiple fields, including immunology, virology, oncology, and infectious diseases, as well as the design of therapeutic antibodies.  Unfortunately, due to the scope and technical complexity of this work, certain aspects of the methodology had to be omitted from the main text, and these crucial details can be found in the appended supplementary materials.  To ensure the continued accessibility and usability of the results presented here, we have made all relevant data and software resources available online as part of this study.  As a culmination of this research, we present a comprehensive framework and computational tool that can simulate the crystal structures of antibodies within lattice assemblies, and this knowledge is applied to the analysis of over 6,000 unique antibodies, yielding novel insights into the complex assembly and antigen recognition mechanisms of antibodies.  By further developing this research, we aim to explore the possibility of designing multi-protein structures through the study of antibody assemblies, and this understanding can be utilized to inform the design of therapeutic antibodies. infected with HIV-1, a virus that infects and replicates within the human immune CD4+ T cell, and then infects a new host through various transmission routes. Despite advanced antiretroviral therapies, HIV-1 eventually reactivates from latent forms and causes AIDS, the deadliest form of the disease. Understanding how HIV-1 interacts with its host's cells and selects targets for infection, especially in the presence of antivirals that block one such interaction, is a complex task. To tackle this, we developed a mathematical model of how HIV-1 infects and replicates within a single host over time, incorporating over 200 separate statistical analyses to estimate unknown variables and test model predictions. Using this model, we analyzed how HIV-1 chooses which cells to infect, the impact of antiviral-resistant mutations on this, and the role of CD4+ T cell depletion in shaping infection dynamics. Our results confirm existing theories on how HIV-1 selects targets for infection, while also yielding new predictions and insights to guide both epidemiological modeling and biomedical research. By providing a detailed explanation of how HIV-1 infects and replicates within a single host, our model can be applied to study other chronic and persistent infections. 

  The code used for data fitting, simulation, and plotting in this research is available for download at the specified URL. 

  The HIV-1 infection model we developed accounts for various processes and variables involved in the infection, including the total number of uninfected and infected CD4+ T cells, the product of infection probability and cell susceptibility, the rate of cell activation and replication, the rate of antiviral-resistant mutation emergence and fixation, the rate of latent cell reactivation and infection, and the rate of infected cell death. 

  Based on previously published data, we conducted separate statistical analyses to estimate no less than one hundred unknown variables and parameters that define HIV-1 infection dynamics in its host. 

  The results of our analysis confirmed key predictions of the model, revealed new insights on the mechanisms driving HIV-1 selection and epidemiology, and provided a detailed explanation of how HIV-1 chooses which cells to infect, which is critical for developing both effective antiviral therapies and prevention methods.

behavior of a complex, time-dependent wave function in a finite square well potential with rigid walls, under a constant external electric field. We have determined the essential conditions for a wave function to be stable, and the parameters which define its stability. We have analyzed the effects of the external electric field on energy levels and wave functions, and we have derived explicit, infinite series expressions for both the average energy and the stability parameters, under this influence. We have also compared our series results with simple, yet accurate, "hydrogenic" models, and we have established the parameters at which these models lose their validity. Finally, we have discussed the implications of our findings on the behavior of atoms and molecules in vacuum spaces, and we have highlighted the importance of considering both the ground and excited states of a system when measuring its stability.  No new conclusions are drawn from the results presented in this study. neural networks has been a challenge, especially when it comes to characterizing their ability to approximate other functions. This study focuses on a specific aspect of this issue - the complexity of functions represented by neural networks with binary weights. We establish a key finding regarding the approximation capacity of binary neural networks, demonstrating that any function representable by a binary neural network can also be represented by a neural network with continuous weights that has a significantly reduced parameter count, specifically O(log^3 n) times fewer parameters than the original binary network, where n represents the number of input dimensions. This result demonstrates that the ability to approximate continuous functions using binary neural networks corresponds to an equivalent capability in continuous neural networks with an significantly reduced parameter count. This equivalence holds both for bounded and unbounded functions, and is established through a novel technique that involves a customized decoding function with log^3 n multiplicative factors, which enables the conversion of binary networks into their equivalent continuous versions. This discovery is further showcased through concrete examples involving step and threshold activation functions, as well as discussions on potential applications and open research avenues for binary neural networks. Finally, our theory comes paired with easy-to-implement approximation algorithms for the continuous equivalent networks. 

  From a practical standpoint, our results indicate that any function computable by a binary neural network can also be computed by a neural network with an enormously reduced parameter count (e.g. millions of parameters versus just 54 for a 10-dimensional input), which may have significant implications for the study of deep learning and neural network structure. 

  This research employs a novel technique that involves a customized decoding function with enormous multiplicative factors to demonstrate the equivalence of binary and continuous neural networks. 

  Our findings establish the equivalence of two challenging problems: reaching an arbitrarily low error rate on a specific problem vs. achieving an arbitrarily low complexity class for a specific function, which may have significant implications. 

  This research is further showcased through concrete examples and accompanied by easy-to-implement approximation algorithms for the continuous equivalent networks. 

  Finally, our results open up several research avenues for binary neural networks, as well as intricate problems that are now known to be equivalent to reachable error rates.

However, this method has a significant drawback - it requires knowledge of the underlying space's structure. In contrast, the Vittorini-Menger metric offers an alternative approach that focuses directly on set-distance relationships, establishing a link between sets and the structure of the underlying space in which they are defined. This paper delves into the specifics of this metric, particularly its relationship with the Hausdorff metric, examining how it behaves in different types of spaces. This problem is resolved by the model for estimated suboptimal samples (MESS), which pins down a limited set of samples likely to maximize model performance with minimal supervision.  MESS does this by leveraging a latent variable model that simultaneously estimates both the effectiveness of each sample in improving model accuracy and the underlying structure of the data's annotation process. We show that a unique, efficient method can be used to train all neural network models with squared error loss functions, specifically doing away with the need for stochastic gradient descent and related optimization techniques. This involves leveraging a particular weighted average of past training data, which we demonstrate is equivalent to a fixed point of the network's expectation propagation algorithm. This weight update rule allows for significantly faster training times and greater accuracy when testing. &D detectors for the ILC are primarily constrained by two factors: the relatively high noise levels in their readout systems and the constraints of their low-exposure data sets. To simulate the characteristics of future detectors more accurately, the R&D phase should be extended to include prototypes built with components similar to those used in the actual detectors. These prototypes should be developed using advanced readout systems and taking into consideration the vast amounts of data that can be collected at the ILC. In this context, we propose a design for a prototype silicon detector that incorporates an ASIC designed for digital readout, where each hit is converted to a logical bit and converted to an analog value using an analog-to-digital converter. This approach allows for a significant reduction in hit detection thresholds and the effective lowering of leakage equivalent noise. We have tested a previous version of this ASIC, known as CEC, which demonstrated a low hit threshold of 150 electrons. Building on this experience, we have designed a new ASIC, referred to as CECv2, which incorporates an improved power management system to minimize power supply fluctuations that could compromise the detector's performance. By utilizing a power supply rejection ratio of approximately 100 dB, this new ASIC should be capable of achieving even lower hit thresholds. In addition, we have simulated hit detection performances at various leakage currents, achieving hit thresholds of 100 and 150 electrons for 1 $\mu$s and 10 $\mu$s exposure times, respectively. With the CECv2 prototype silicon detector having reached hit thresholds of 150 electrons in our laboratory tests, we believe it is ready to be taken to the square kilometer scale for use in the ILC. With integrated digital readout and a low hit threshold, this detector is well-suited to provide maximum utility from ILC data, especially when coupled with future R&D detectors that will be capable of collecting vast amounts of data at the ILC. Furthermore, we propose a multi-ASIC module design that incorporates four CECv2 ASICs, along with a multi-analog-to-digital converter (ADC) board capable of handling up to 1024 hits per clock cycle, or approximately 1.8 billion hits per second. With this design, we have calculated hit detection performance figures of merit (PFT) for various hit thresholds and exposure times, and have also simulated hit detection performance for various hit thresholds, achieving hit thresholds of 100 and 150 electrons for 1 $\mu$s and 10 $\mu$s exposure times, respectively. A line emission spectrum, characteristic of gas within the galaxy's center, shows variations in the [O III]$λ$5007 and H$β$ line strengths and shapes that cannot be explained by the effects of star formation. These line variations are interpreted as physical changes within the galaxy's central region due to a massive, gas-rich binary black hole with a 432 parsec separation and orbital periods of 13 to 46 years, depending on mass. This finding aligns with the hypothesis that massive galaxies contain binary black holes and provides an opportunity to study their interactions through gas emission lines. Observations also reveal an intrinsic line shift of 13 to 34 kilometers per second within the galaxy, which can be interpreted as evidence of gas moving between the two black holes or gas orbiting one of the black holes. The mass of the binary black hole system is estimated to be greater than 10,000 times the mass of the sun, with a ratio of black hole to host galaxy mass similar to that of other massive galaxies. The absence of X-ray emission from the galaxy and its stellar population suggests that its binary black hole is in a quiescent state, offering a unique opportunity to study the system through optical emission lines over the next several decades as it approaches closest approach. The absence of a significant nucleus and the presence of a central ionized gas component make NGC 4365 an appropriate comparison galaxy for observations of the Milky Way using radio and next-generation telescopes. The dynamics of the galaxy suggest that its binary black hole is likely responsible for the generation of radio waves from the galaxy, which may indicate that the binary black hole in the Milky Way is also responsible for the detection of radio waves in our galaxy. The presence of a binary black hole within NGC 4365 also makes the galaxy an ideal target for the detection of gravitational waves through the interaction of its binary black hole and a candidate for a intermediate-mass black hole found within the galaxy's core. We propose a novel application of noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) computers in quantum research, leveraging their ability to conduct approximate version verification efficiently. Our research also suggests the potential for NISQ computers to tackle complex, real-world problems in quantum research, such as testing the universality of quantum light-matter systems and calculating quantum circuit noise resilience. This variable-bounded complexity theory result has implications for the study of quantifier reasoning within first-order and higher-order logic. It demonstrates that any algorithm capable of handling complex quantifier structures can be thought of as a sum of simpler components, each focused on handling a specific variable-based situation. This framework allows us to examine basic vs. composite cases of quantifier structure, variable-bounded combinations of instances, and more. As an example, solving satisfiability in prenex normal form corresponds to handling combinations of instances, which can be seen as a combination of purely positive cases. This perspective appears first in a 1993 paper by Bachmair and Gribbrock, but with limited scope. Our work expands and formalizes these ideas within the context of higher-order logic, building on advances in first-order logic since the original 1989 paper by Bachmair and Gribbrock. 

  Specifically, we establish a hierarchy of satisfiability problems in prenex normal form with zero to multiple distinct variables, mirroring the structure of the corresponding quantifier prefixes. Each level in this hierarchy contains problems that require vastly different approaches to solve, as there's no common algorithm capable of solving any two such problems efficiently. This result showcases the complexity of certain higher-order satisfiability problems and provides a variable-bounded complexity theory framework that can be applied to study both first-order and higher-order logic. 

  Furthermore, our theory includes multiple combinators for combining instances of satisfiability problems in specific contexts, such as combining positive cases or situations with particular variable properties. This allows us to examine the relationships between various combinations of instances and their corresponding combined satisfiability problems. 

  As an example, solving any combination of instances with particular variable properties reduces to solving discrete satisfiability problems in corresponding matrices, which can be seen as discrete combination problems of instances with the same variable properties. 

  This perspective on higher-order satisfiability problems provides a variable-bounded complexity theory framework that can be used to study both first-order and higher-order logic, and demonstrates that key results in first-order logic, such as the hierarchy of prenex normal form satisfiability problems, can be derived within this framework.

The study focuses on the impact of using different fluid flow models - either constant velocity or mathematically defined velocity - on mass transfer from the cylinder. Unlike previous studies, where the velocity is kept constant and uniform, the new approach reveals that increasing the cylinder's radius will eventually lead to a decrease in mass transfer rates. This decrease is attributed to the accumulation of concentration boundary layers around the cylinder. These findings provide new insights into the complex fluid flow and mass transfer interactions surrounding the composite cylinder. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that using a level set method, combined with the Dirac-Delta function, accurately represents mass transfer from the composite cylinder. Based on these results, we propose an simplified approach to estimate mass transfer rates. The new model includes parameters such as the radius of the non-penetrable core and the ratio of the outer to inner cylinder radii. These findings have the potential to contribute to the understanding and mitigation of clogging phenomena in flow filtration systems. Furthermore, the study highlights the necessity of employing more sophisticated flow models when modeling composite cylinders, and suggests possible applications to tubes with embedded particles or fibers.

observed around young stars is caused by a shock ring formed by a rapidly spinning star. We use three-dimensional hydrodynamic simulations to study this phenomenon, focusing on how it's affected by the star's rotation rate and the presence of magnetic fields. Our findings reveal that a shock wave is generated at a distance from the star where its rotational energy converts to thermal energy, producing a disc cavity. The presence of magnetic fields, whether they're globally symmetrical or asymmetrical, doesn't significantly alter the shape of the cavity. However, magnetic fields can create a thinner, more curved disc around certain cases, but this doesn't align with observed data. We also find that a shock ring can form even if the star isn't entirely surrounded by a disc, but this depends on the rate at which it spins and the amount of matter in the disc that's affected by the star's gravitational force. Our model can already accurately match observed photospheric flux variations, but it lacks the power to explain all observed phenomena around young stars. Further research is needed to fully understand and apply this model to real stars. 

  We also introduce a new simple model for disc accretion, as well as a new method for calculating the star's rotational energy, which can be used to observe a star's rotation rate and the characteristics of its surrounding disc. These models and methods may be useful for studying and comparing real stars with those in our simulations. 

  Our study confirms that a disc cavity is created at a distance from the star that's proportional to its rotation rate, which is essential for comparing simulated results with real stars in the T Tauri phase, but it doesn't fully address all aspects of the Accretion Boundary Layer. 

  We also explore the possibility of directly detecting a shock ring and the disc cavity through indirect imaging techniques like PALM-2000/NACO, which may provide a way to observe the disc structure around young stars more clearly, as well as the effects of their rotational energy, the presence of magnetic fields, and the behavior of the inner disc on their appearance. 

  Our research highlights the importance of running high-resolution, three-dimensional simulations that take into account the star's rotational energy, as well as the characteristics of the inner disc and the behavior of the Accretion Boundary Layer, in order to provide a complete and accurate view of the disc structure around young stars, which can be used to explain all observed phenomena and provide a clear basis for comparing real stars with those in our simulations.

Due to the lack of a causal storage policy, we cannot optimize intermediate storage usage. Therefore, we focus on optimizing the first-stage storage usage subject to rate constraints in each stage. We have developed a general approach for solving this problem with non-causal storage policies, including the specific case of multi-stage distributed storage systems with no causal storage policies. Specifically, we derive an efficient algorithm for finding the optimal first-stage storage usage that meets rate constraints in each stage and minimizes the overall storage cost. This algorithm has important implications for the design of distributed storage systems used in video caching, over-the-top services, and internet content. It enables service providers to optimize first-stage storage usage, which significantly affects the performance, in exchange for a limited increase in storage cost. We also present numerical results that demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in designing distributed storage systems. Furthermore, we investigate the problem of maximizing the service lifetime of a single resource, such as a video, by optimizing the first-stage storage usage. This problem cannot be solved efficiently by standard methods. propose a new way to define a second-order curvature quantity, called the 'curvature image', for any given function u within a target domain G. The curvature image is related to the p-dimensional analog of the Fisher Information Matrix and can be computed through a linear operation on the gradient of u, where the operator is defined by the p-dimensional Hausdorff-Young Inequality. When the target domain G is a flat space, we demonstrate that our curvature image formulation is equivalent to that of Daniilidis and others. However, our formulation also applies to curved spaces, where the curvature image is represented by a matrix whose properties are characterized by a generalized Fisher Information Matrix. We then leverage this formulation to develop a new efficient algorithm for solving second-order convex optimization problems of the type min_{u} \int_G u^p dx + \lambda [u]_* where [u]_* represents the optimal transport cost. This algorithm is based on an iterative update rule involving the curvature image and leads to a rate of convergence of O(1/k^2) for its stationary point iterations. Notably, our approach is highly versatile and can be applied to a broad class of functions u, further enriching the domain of optimization problems that can be efficiently solved using optimal transport methods. The algorithm's effectiveness is demonstrated through numerical experiments conducted on diverse examples spanning various application areas. The theoretical convergence rate of O(1/k^2) is proven by leveraging a generalized Bregman distance and its associated properties. The algorithm's coordinator component is an accelerated version of the Fienberg-McLennan algorithm, where the rate of convergence for one of its sub-problems is set to O(1/k^2). The algorithm also includes an efficient sampling scheme, an accelerated version of the hit-and-miss algorithm, with a rate of convergence of O(1/k^2) for solving a specific type of convex optimization problem. The algorithm's coordinator and sampler are robust to over-parameterization, hyper-parameter free, and require only a fixed number of iterations that is proportional to the dimension of the target domain G as well as the number of grid points used to approximate the Kurzweg measure. To address this challenge, we propose a detoxification filter that screens task instructions for potentially harmful content. This filter is distinct from instruction normalization, which aims to normalize instructional variations to enhance learning stability. Instead, the detoxification filter aims to ensure the coding model's safety by preventing harmful instructions from influencing model performance. To investigate this mechanism further, a perovskite solar cell material was studied at the atomic level during operation, using temporal atomic phase analysis of scanning tunneling microscopy images.  computational requirements make it an ideal solution for healthcare providers and

code for the proposed method has been made available for public use.  Although the 
paper utilizes EHR as a primary example, the authentication framework can be 
flexibly applied to other sensitive systems necessitating high security.

genuine login activities from real-world datasets such as Google's Charlette-7 and 
Mnist.  The results show our method outperforms existing classification approaches

  * For genus greater than one, an embedded torus in a three-dimensional manifold with non-negative curvature can be smoothly deformed into another torus of the same genus, providing a one-parameter family of surfaces that includes the original one.
  * For genus two, an embedded torus in a three-dimensional manifold with non-negative curvature can be parameterized using two independent angles from its boundary, indicating that its Euler characteristic is two.

  These results expand upon a relevant theorem proved by Souillet, addressing embedded tori of a given genus in a three-dimensional manifold with non-negative curvature.  If the genus is greater than one, the theorem asserts that an embedded torus can be parameterized using one angle from its boundary, indicating that its Euler characteristic is greater than one.  If the genus is two, the theorem asserts that an embedded torus in a three-dimensional manifold with non-negative curvature cannot be smoothly deformed into another torus of the same genus, providing a counterexample to a conjecture originally proposed by Souillet.  This counterexample involves a three-dimensional manifold with a category Horev's property RH2, which can be achieved using a construction first described by Gromov.  This construction involves adding a set of points to a surface, where the points have a specific distance from any point on the surface, effectively creating a nested set of circles.  If the genus is one, an embedded torus in a three-dimensional manifold with non-negative curvature may not be parameterized using an angle from its boundary, as demonstrated by a trefoil knot embedded in a sphere with a curvature of zero.  However, an embedded torus in a three-dimensional manifold with a curvature of zero can be parameterized using one angle from its boundary if it contains a circle as a submanifold, as shown by a torus defined by the parametric equation (cos(u), sin(u), sin(v)).  If the genus is one, an embedded torus in a three-dimensional manifold with non-negative curvature can be smoothly deformed into another torus of the same genus, providing a one-parameter family of surfaces that includes the original one, as demonstrated by a trefoil knot embedded in a sphere with a curvature of zero. Yet, for models with complex parameter spaces and moderate dimensionality, traditional MCMC methods often struggle to achieve a high level of mixing efficiency. This struggle is particularly evident in Bayesian hierarchical models, which incorporate multiple layers of unobserved variables. In such cases, the MCMC trajectories tend to become stuck in localized regions of the parameter space, making the traditional MCMC estimator biased. This issue can be mitigated by using a critical value (VC) that estimates the variance of the MCMC estimator. Current methods for UDA, such as contrastive learning, are often hindered by the challenges of obtaining reliable unlabeled data in various domains and the difficulty of overcoming the domain shift gap. To address this, we develop a novel framework called label propagation and selection (LAPS) that leverages both labeled data in each domain and encourages the generation of domain-invariant representations. LAPS comprises two key components: a graph- based label propagation module and a balanced selection module. The former uses a graph representation learning approach to propagate labels across domains and create a shared representation, while the latter removes noisy labels and selects a balance of hard positive and hard negative examples for training. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by achieving state-of-the-art performance on the domain adaptation version of the mini-ImageNet benchmark, as well as notable improvements on the MSMNIST and semi-supervised domain adaptation version of the OMNIGLOT and 20-Newsgroups datasets. in diverse environments to better detect fraud clicks.

and the underlying operating system can enhance the precision and F1-score 
in identifying fraud clicks.

in e-commerce sponsored search by leveraging training data from common click 
patterns, thereby preventing potential losses.

  Utilizing quark model approaches, we evaluate the impact of $b-s$ wave function mixing
  on the $B_c$ meson mass difference, considering various parameters and their interactions.
  Our calculations show that $b-s$ wave function mixing has a significant effect on the $B_c$

  that the $s$ quark's radial and orbital excitations can contribute substantially to the $B_c$
  meson mass difference.
  Our study also reveals that the $s$ quark's radial excitation in $B_c^*$ significantly
  influences the $B_c$ meson mass difference, with an impact on the $B_c^*$ ground and
  first radial excitation mass difference of about $0.06$ GeV.
  These findings emphasize the importance of considering boson-fermion mixing in flavor-
  focused bound states and the necessity of selecting appropriate quark model parameters. 
  Our research primarily utilizes the MIT bag model, but the results may be applicable to
  other quark model approaches with non-relativistic quark degrees of freedom. 
  Consequently, boson-fermion mixing should be factored into the calculations of quark
  mass splitting within flavor-focused bound states that exhibit significant mixing effects. 
  The impact on the $B_c$ meson mass difference is notable, but the effect on other meson
  systems, such as charmed or bottom strange mesons, is more complex and depends on the
  mixing effects at play. 
  The influence of boson-fermion mixing on the $B_c$ meson mass difference is partially
  compensated by the $s$ quark's radial and orbital excitations, indicating that more
  sophisticated approaches that differentiate between different quark excitations are
  needed to accurately model other meson systems.

exposure and proposal protocols. The Proposal Protocol can be classified into 
two types: it may either always accept the first proposal, or reject proposals 
that suggest less favorable partners than the current one, in which case the 
rejected partner becomes available for further proposal. We investigate the 
relationship between different proposal protocols and their corresponding exposure 
protocols, specifically whether a particular protocol can be achieved through 
another, or if a protocol results in a stable matching where all individuals are 
paired. We also examine the communication costs associated with various protocols. 
We find that the ability to always accept the first proposal does not imply the 
ability to propose in a way that achieves the same matching, but that the reverse 
is true. We show that there is no proposal protocol that can produce the same 
matchings as the Falcon and Eagle protocols, which involve the most extensive 
communication, but that the Frog protocol, which communicates minimally, can be 
achieved through a reasonable proposal protocol.  Finally, we introduce a new 
classification of exposure protocols and use this to demonstrate that all stable 
matchings can be achieved through a specific type of proposal protocol.

Despite its benefits, estimating extreme quantile volatility proves challenging due to the need for very low tail quantiles, which are often difficult to obtain, especially in real-time applications.  This paper presents a non-parametric approach to measuring extreme quantile volatility, which can handle short samples and heavy-tailed data. Results from Monte Carlo simulations show that our proposed method performs well in short samples and heavy-tailed settings.  Furthermore, a real-world application is presented to demonstrate the method's effectiveness in capturing extreme quantile volatility, which was found to be more reliable than conventional measures.  The method's code is made available for public use. 

  Specifically, we employ a long memory model to capture the behavior of conventional conditional variance measures, known as the fractional autoregressive model, which can be estimated via the local Whittle estimator.  An alternative approach involves leveraging the robust properties of the extreme value theory to estimate the density of maximum values without assuming heavy-tailed data.  An empirical component is also investigated where the parameter of the long memory model is estimated via the residual-based method.  Monte Carlo simulations are conducted to evaluate the reliability of the robust density estimator and the reliability of the results when the data is heavy-tailed. 

  The method is demonstrated using stock price returns for 25 European indices to compare the performance of conventional and robust measures of conditional quantile volatility. 

  The analysis reveals that conventional measures prove unreliable in this setting, likely due to the impact of heavy-tailed data on their effectiveness.  In contrast, the robust approach proves successful in capturing extreme quantile volatility accurately. 

  The successful application of this method is likely to be far-reaching, given its utility in evaluating the reliability of conventional conditional variance measures, particularly in contexts characterized by heavy-tailed data. 

  The proposed estimator is also likely to be successful in other financial settings, such as when analyzing the behavior of individual stocks or sectors. 

  The code for the robust density estimator and the results is provided in the supplementary material, along with additional details on the specification of the long memory model and the parameters employed. 

  An extended version of the paper, which includes additional empirical applications and results, is available separately.

on the scattering of light from electrons in microcavity lasers has been analyzed, and our research shows that this phenomenon produces beat waves at specific angles. These beat waves result from the interaction between two light waves generated by space-heterodyne microcavity lasers. We have observed that applying a non-uniform magnetic field significantly affects the amplitude and phase of one of these light waves, while the other remains unaffected, and that the beat wave can be optimized by adjusting the magnitude of the magnetic field. Furthermore, our findings indicate that microcavity lasers can provide a reliable source of beat waves, and that this phenomenon is magnified by the high gain inherent to these lasers. Our research also suggests that electron optics designed to maximize beat wave amplitude may compromise phase stability, and that further study is needed to resolve this issue. However, our measurements demonstrate the potential of microcavity lasers to generate beat waves, and that this phenomenon can be adjusted by modifying the magnetic field strength. For example, applying a 103.5 kG magnetic field to our laser system results in beat waves with an amplitude of up to 5 times the standard deviation of the background noise, and a frequency of approximately 7.8 GHz, which can be induced in beams of electrons with energies between 15 and 25 MeV. The generation of beat waves in this research has been observed in two types of microcavity lasers featuring different optical designs, and the findings indicate that the effect of the magnetic field on the light wave can be optimized to match the beat frequency of the laser. This limitation stems from a fundamental challenge in representing the parse tree hierarchy through a linear model. To overcome this constraint, we propose a novel approach, based on a neural network, that incorporates a unique hierarchical representation of tree structures. This approach uses a directed acyclic graph (DAG) to model the extended contextual dependencies within a sentence. Moreover, we develop a new algorithm to generate the DAG representation of the parse tree by identifying and traversing the contextual dependencies indicated by the shift/reduce actions during parsing. This algorithm enables a single-model to achieve high-orbit performance on both simple and complex sentences, outperforming existing multi-model approaches. Experimental evaluations on multiple standard datasets show our proposed approach consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance. This work provides a new perspective on neural dependency parsing, unlocking the door for further research on the contextual dependencies within a sentence. Since the proposed approach uses a fixed-size parameter vector to represent the context of each word, we also explore extending this design to incorporate more contextual information, leading to significant performance gains. Words can have different linguistic roles, such as affecting dependencies or parsing difficulties, which are captured in word embeddings. However, since the embeddings are frozen during training, we investigate reweighting the importance of these representations in inference. This work demonstrates that by assigning weights proportional to the softmax of the embeddings in relation to the parse label cluster centers, the performance of the model is greatly enhanced with no additional parameters. Following this design, we achieve our best result of 42.4 parse score on the CoNLL 2005 English data with a single-model setup, outperforming multi-model approaches by a significant margin. This weight assignment strategy is versatile, applying to both tree-based and graph-based dependencies, as well as to neural and non-neural parsing models. Moreover, we release our code and model checkpoints to facilitate future research and replication. Despite being a vital component, the jet stream's role in this dynamic has been understated, likely due to the stream's meridional variability hindering previous research. Recent studies have discovered a strong correlation between the jet stream's position and temperature anomalies in the stratosphere. While a link exists between these features in the troposphere, their relationship in the stratosphere is less clear. Utilizing a 12-year dataset from the ERA-Interim reanalysis, as well as a statistical model called the Quantum Conditional Ensemble, researchers have found a distinct temporal structure in the stratospheric temperature anomalies. This structure was then applied to a 20-year period spanning 2000 to 2020. The results showed the anomalies in the mid-latitude stratosphere during boreal summer being ~3000 km long and extending from 100 K to 5 K. A further breakdown revealed that the longer the stream, the cooler the temperature within the wave guide. Interestingly, this relationship was not constant and varied significantly between 30-day periods. It was also discovered as well as previous findings, that the stream's position had a profound effect on temperature in the stratosphere. However, the extent to which the jet stream influenced temperature within the wave guide ranged from minimal to extreme, indicating that other factors could play a crucial role, possibly even changing the circulation's response. The research demonstrated that the larger the wave guide, the longer the stream, the greater the risk of temperature dropping below 2 K. This 2 K threshold may indicate an increased likelihood of stratospheric polar cooling and its associated impact on mid-latitude temperature anomalies. The findings also suggested that the stream's impact could either enhance or diminish the amplification of temperature with elevation, potentially because of varying circulation types, such as breaking waves and frontal activity. The research provided a starting point for investigating the complex relationship between the jet stream and temperature in the stratosphere, offering opportunities for further exploration using ensemble analysis.
