covalent bond stretching, angle bending, and torsion contributions have been widely employed for approximately 50 years in molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. Unfortunately, this simplistic approach fails to accurately represent chemical bonds in ions and rare gas molecules, and also cannot capture any deviations from linearity in molecular angles or perfect periodicity in molecular chains. To address these limitations, we propose augmented classical force fields (AFC) that build on the foundation of CC, by adding ad hoc harmonic constraints to constrain the variables that bond, angle, and torsion approximations failed to accurately represent initially. These harmonic constraints are subtly connected to the initial CC potential energy function, thus ensuring that they don't alter the equilibrium properties of the system. As a result, AFCs offer a direct solution to the issues plaguing the traditional force fields, and our examples showcase their utilization in simulating rare gas clusters and molecular crystals. By leveraging harmonic constraints to rectify the shortcomings of CC approximations, AFCs provide a straightforward path to enhancing the accuracy and reliability of MD simulations. 

  Furthermore, harmonic constraints can also be utilized to enhance machine learning potentials, where AFCs serve as a bridge between the atomistic and training data levels. By employing harmonic constraints to model the variables that CC approximations failed to accurately represent, MD-20, our example, demonstrates how this strategy can be applied to simulate rare gas systems with ions. 

  In conclusion, the augmented classical force fields present an incredibly cost-effective solution to enhancing the accuracy and reliability of MD simulations in chemistry and materials science, and we anticipate this method to have a significant impact on the field in the years to come. 

  Additionally, this method can also facilitate the development of more precise machine learning potentials, and we anticipate seeing applications of the AFC-MLP combination in the near future. 

  Finally, the source code for the examples discussed in this work, which involves rare gas clusters and molecular crystals simulated using harmonic constraints in AFCs based on MM, is publicly available for use and further development. 

  We look forward to seeing AFCs continuing to contribute to advancements in the field of molecular dynamics, and are happy to provide guidance and support to researchers and students who may utilize this method in the future. 

  In particular, we anticipate seeing applications of the AFC-MLP combination, and are willing to share our experience and expertise with researchers who may utilize this method in the years to come.

This paper employs analytical and experimental methods to explore the motion of walking robots.  By recognizing that movement is most simply defined as a periodic walk, we can analyze locomotion through the properties of this periodic walk. It was also observed that a phenomenon known as contact rotation occurs during locomotion, which is characterized by the rotation of the swing leg during contact with the ground. The Dynamic Complexity framework combines dynamic proof systems with complexity theory to investigate the complexity of ordered structures. The aim of this survey is to summarize the advancements made in this field, focusing on first-order theories of arithmetic and fragments of arithmetic with limited quantifier capacity. The survey examines the proof systems' length and the properties of structures with limited length, as well as the relationship between dynamic complexity and traditional complexity measures. The discussion covers recent advances in research on the propositional version of Dynamic Complexity and its implications for the complexity of ordered structures. The survey also includes an introduction to the concept of a'structure of proofs', which provides a more comprehensive understanding of first-order dynamic complexity. The survey covers research published up to March 2022. The topics covered include but are not limited to:
  - Dynamic complexity in the context of first-order theories of arithmetic and fragments of arithmetic with limited quantifier capacity
  - The relationship between first-order dynamic complexity and the length of proofs in corresponding systems of formal reasoning
  - The relationship between first-order dynamic complexity and the properties of structures with limited length
  - The connection between first-order and propositional dynamic complexity

In the strong field limit, the wave functions' behavior becomes highly complex and irregular, especially with increasing angular momentum. This test can be extended to accommodate two non-negative variable sets with any level of abstraction, making it suitable for identifying the correlation between two variables whose relationship may be partially explained by other factors.  In particular, this test has been effective in discovering the link between the number of incoming links to a website and its popularity, as well as the association between file sizes and execution times in mobile applications.  Unlike other correlation tests, Spearman's rank correlation test does not assume a linear relationship between the variables, which makes it more versatile and suitable for analyzing discrete data.  Although more robust methods such as Pearson's correlation coefficient exist, they are only applicable to linear data relationships and typically require smaller datasets to produce accurate results.  In contrast, Spearman's rank correlation test is more flexible and requires larger datasets to produce reliable results.  By comparing the ranks of data pairs instead of their actual values, this test reduces the impact of outliers, making it more suitable for analyzing a wide range of data scenarios.  In addition, the test is an indicator of the dependence between variables, which can be an important factor to consider when designing random mechanisms, as it measures how changes to one variable affect the other variable.  In our experience, this test has consistently produced reliable and accurate results in various scenarios and datasets.  We have used it to analyze the correlation between discrete data sets in multiple projects, including one where websites used search engines and another where mobile application users were categorized by usage time.  We found the test to provide consistent and trustworthy outcomes in these instances and many more.  In particular, we employed the test to examine the connection between website popularity and the number of links to that website, as well as the connection between application execution times and file sizes.  In each of these scenarios and many more, the test consistently yielded reliable and accurate results.   private models.

  data distributions.

  private model converges at the same rate as the non-private model, 
  specifically O(1/\sqrt{T}).

Unlike the photon sphere in the Reissner-Nordstr\"om black hole, which occurs at a singular point, the photon sphere in this charged black hole is circumscribed by an elliptical path. Moreover, as the cosmological constant becomes more negative, the photon sphere moves closer to the event horizon, and its shape is more significantly affected when the charge approaches its maximum value, where the photon sphere assumes an almost circular form. Conversely, in scenarios where the charge is less than its maximum value, the extremal surface connected to the photon sphere exhibits a helical pattern. Notably, this phenomenon does not occur in the Reissner-Nordstr\"om black hole. The appearance of the de Sitter cosmological constant causes a divergence in the radius of the photon sphere at the point of maximum charge, which is analogous to the divergence in the radius of the horizon due to the charge itself. Additionally, the influence of the de Sitter cosmological constant leads to a variation in the shadow radius with charge, displaying an abrupt increase at the point of maximum charge. This study enhances the model by incorporating delays into the equations, reflecting the real-world phenomenon of infected individuals requiring a certain period to infect others. The aim of this research is to examine the stability of the equilibrium points of the delayed system, in order to understand how the appearance of delays affects the non-linear system's behaviour. The model and its analysis are applied to a specific epidemic scenario involving a susceptible-infective-recovered (SIR) model, and the results show how the introduction of delays affects the model's linearised equations. Importantly, this research demonstrates how the stability of the equilibrium points changes with increasing delays, and the resulting conditions which cause the system to become unstable. The impact of these unstable conditions is then discussed in the context of a recent chickenpox outbreak in Wales, UK. The findings indicate that a significant increase in the incidence rate of the disease is caused by the failure of the model to capture the period required for infected individuals to become sources of infection, and how this leads to overstated and fluctuating estimates of the active epidemic. The study also compares itself to a relevant epidemic model presented in a prior paper, and highlights key differences between the two models and their results. Finally, the implications of the research are explored in terms of their policy relevance, and the recommendations are made for the cautious use of mathematical models in informing epidemic control policies. network-based approaches to identifying side-channel attacks on convolutional neural networks (CNNs), particularly focusing on an attack aimed at malware detection.  Initially, we used a publicly available dataset for malware, where it was observed that a side-channel, namely the file size, considerably hinders the malware detection process.  To counter this, we explored three diverse strategies to circumvent the file-size side-channel effect on CNNs.  Our experiments employed two additional, relatively small datasets for natural language processing (NLP) tasks.  In each case, we compared the performance of malware detection systems against both a clean dataset and one contaminated by the file-size side-channel, utilizing multiple evaluation metrics including the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC).  Our key findings indicated that the proposed techniques successfully mitigated the file-size side-channel effect on the malware detection system.  Additionally, we analyzed the relationship between the accuracy of the malware detection system and the file-size side-channel effect, observing that the proposed techniques maintained high accuracy even in the presence of the side-channel, whereas the original system was severely impacted.  Notably, our approach is versatile and applicable to other NLP tasks.  To facilitate replication and advancement of this work, we have made the source code and dataset available for download.  The developed techniques may find utility in enhancing the robustness of machine learning models against side-channels in various contexts.  Furthermore, we have published the paper, which includes our methodology and results, in accordance with the CRC 117 project guidelines.  Specifically, this work aligns with task 3.4, which involves analyzing the impact of side-channels on deep learning models and exploring methods to mitigate these effects.  As part of our research, we proposed three approaches to counter the file-size side-channel effect on CNNs, evaluated them using three datasets, and found that the suggested techniques successfully reduced the impact of the side-channel effect, resulting in system accuracy comparable to that achieved with a clean dataset.  Our work extends previous studies on the security of machine learning models, which typically focus on data privacy and artificial neural network robustness, by investigating side-channel effects that arise from the inherent properties of datasets utilized in NLP tasks.  We investigated three diverse neural network-based approaches to identify side-channel attacks on convolutional neural networks (CNNs), particularly focusing on an attack aimed at malware detection, and successfully developed three techniques that successfully reduced the impact of the side-channel effect, resulting in system accuracy comparable to that achieved with a clean dataset.

COVID-19 pandemic began, there has been a 
  significant increase in the spread of misinformation regarding the virus 
  and available healthcare information. This rise in misinformation has led 
  several researchers to focus on understanding the current information 
  landscape and identifying false health information circulating on the 
  internet. As an initial step to addressing this issue, we present a 
  preliminary analysis of the geographical distribution of published 
  scientific articles and website content regarding COVID-19 by utilizing 
  NLP techniques to examine the credibility of this information. Our study 
  utilizes a NLP model to evaluate the credibility of website content based 
  on the tone, style, and format of each webpage, combined with the 
  application of Bayesian classification to identify credible sources. Our 
  findings reveal a non-uniform distribution of published scientific articles 
  and website content concerning COVID-19 across different regions of 
  Brazil. Furthermore, our results indicate a variety of credible and 
  non-credible content concerning COVID-19, with some themes being
  consistently associated with credible sources and others with
  non-credible ones. Additionally, our analysis across different time
  periods showed a shift in the tone of online content regarding COVID-19
  from objective to emotive as the pandemic progressed, with a
  significant increase in the use of slang and neologisms during this
  period. Our study's methodology and results have the potential to
  contribute to ongoing research and monitoring of the information
  landscape regarding COVID-19 and other future health crises.

This research aims to develop a reliable portfolio optimization framework that withstands market volatility and unpredictability by minimizing risk and maximizing returns. For this purpose, we first identify suitable risk management metrics among various existing ones, ultimately selecting Value-at-Risk (VaR) as the most suitable for our analysis. We then propose a novel approach to estimate the tail risks associated with multiple randomly generated portfolios, thereby evaluating the performance of our optimal portfolio. In addition, we establish a threshold to determine whether a portfolio's risk levels are acceptable, using this criterion to differentiate between low-risk and high-risk portfolios. In our experiments, we demonstrate that our proposed approach outperforms the naive diversification strategy, observing that the low-risk portfolios resulted in a 3.6% lower risk level and 5.4% higher returns compared to the naive approach. Furthermore, our results indicate that the risk levels associated with randomly generated portfolios are significantly higher than those of our optimal portfolio, supporting the effectiveness of our proposed optimization technique.

When data is structured along a linear structure, such as in graphs or chains, the choice of propagation path can significantly impact the learning speed and model quality. Nonetheless, determining the optimal path is computationally expensive and may vary throughout the training process. We investigate the possibility of assigning different weights to the potential paths at the beginning of training, with the aim of ensuring that the assigned weights reflect the relative performance of each path and can be applied safely across multiple training iterations. We develop a simple yet effective method for updating the assigned weights based on the performance of a randomly selected batch, and demonstrate that this approach leads to improved performance when learning on linear structures. The improvement is particularly noticeable in environments with limited or unstable connectivity. Additionally, the proposed method yields noticeable benefits in scenarios where data is divided horizontally, due to its higher sensitivity to the estimation of communication gradients. We evaluate our method on a variety of scenarios involving both horizontal and vertical data division, using various communication schedules, and find that it results in significant improvements over baseline approaches. By adjusting a symmetry breaking parameter related to the orientation of the crystal, we achieve zero energy Majorana modes without incorporating magnetic fields.  Additionally, we investigate the impact of spin-orbit coupling on the zero energy modes and find that a specific rotation of the spinor can be compensated for by adjusting the symmetry breaking parameter, thus identifying a range of (110) oriented GaAs/Al heterostructures where Majorana modes can be achieved with minimal spin-orbit coupling.  Our study provides practical guidance for realizing Majorana modes in GaAs-based systems.  Furthermore, we propose an experimental protocol to determine the spin-orbit coupling strength in these systems, involving a measurement of the zero bias conductance at the ends of a nanowire and the associated backscattering process induced by a bound magnon in an Al gap layer.  A specific strength of a few tenths of a millielectronvolt serves as the distinguishing factor between two types of zero energy modes resulting from spin-orbit coupling, with isolable Majorana modes achievable when this parameter is under this threshold value.  We show that a majorana hybridization gap, a distinctive signature of the interaction between two isolated Majorana modes, can be converted into a conductance gap in a $p$-shell of an aligned Ga/Al heterostructure, thereby providing a method to detect this effect experimentally.  By comparing two approaches to realize Majorana mode, a GaAs core Al shell nanowire and a GaAs/(110) Al heterostructure, we find that GaAs core Al shell nanowire will face a hybridization gap problem, which will not occur in an aligned Ga/Al heterostructure, providing an advantage for the latter in detecting the majorana hybridization gap effect.  Our study enables the selection of material orientations that minimize spin-orbit coupling to achieve robust Majorana modes and provides the basis for the development of electronic devices that detect the majorana hybridization gap effect, with outcomes that can be verified experimentally.  We also examine whether pairing of zero energy modes can be driven by luminescence coupling between two Al layers separated by a GaAs gap layer, with the outcome dependent on the orientation of the crystal, with d-wave and s-wave pairing corresponding to (110) and (100) orientations, respectively. Nevertheless, the emergence of cyberphysical systems in smart grids introduces critical security vulnerabilities that threaten to disrupt their operation. Presently, there is a pressing need to adapt optimal control methods that can handle the complex, highly interconnected nature of grid dynamics. This paper outlines a novel approach to tracking area control contributions using differential games, which can be solved using a robust controller that meets specific safety and performance objectives. The proposed method involves approximating the game's solution using a set of robust control Lyapunov functions, which enables the derivation of upper and lower bounds on the time it takes to achieve a desired state. Furthermore, this approach enables the generation of secure trajectories for the control centers' state and output variables, which can be utilized in real-time autonomous operations. A case study on the IEEE 24-node reliability index grid demonstrates the efficacy of the proposed robust controller in ensuring the safe and efficient operation of smart grids. Ultimately, this work provides a novel solution to an ongoing research challenge and paves the way for the development of advanced autonomous control systems that can collaborate with utilities and prosumers through the implementation of robust optimal control policies. Nevertheless, the selection of robust control Lyapunov functions via genetic algorithms remains an open issue that requires further exploration. Despite this, the proposed approach has already been successfully integrated into the autonomous operation framework of a real-world utility company in the United States. The code supplied with this paper has been employed by this utility in a preliminary setup, where it has successfully guided the control centers' state and output variables towards desired secure trajectories during various test scenarios. Andrews created a set of numbers that, along with their variants, possess a remarkable property - they fully classify the multiplicity of generic singularities in two dimensions. These numbers have since been referred to as the Speyer-Andrews numbers. Within this study, we aim to establish a more direct link between these numbers and the actual multiplicity of singularities, rather than their generic form. To do this, we'll first demonstrate that the classical Speyer-Andrews numbers can be employed to determine the algebraic degree of a singularity. Next, we'll show the same numbers can also indicate the length of the singularity's ring. Having achieved this, the differences between classical and extended Speyer-Andrews numbers become more apparent, as they now reflect the distinct relationships they hold with the singularity's ring and its factors. Lastly, we'll utilize these newfound connections to derive several important results stemming from the current research, including conclusions about singularities with specific characteristics and the behavior of their variants. Overall, this study serves as a starting point to explore the broader implications of Speyer-Andrews numbers within the context of singularities.  This work is an extension of the authors' previous research presented in Preprints arXiv:2112.09531 and arXiv:2112.09532.  Due to time constraints, the discussion on Corollary 4.13 has been omitted from the current presentation.  After the initial submission, further observations led to an updated understanding of the relationship between classical Speyer-Andrews numbers, the algebraic degree of a singularity, and its defining equation.  It is now known that the classical Speyer-Andrews numbers actually determine the degree of the singularities' equation, rather than their algebraic degree as previously believed.  This newfound insight along with other key findings are being considered for an upcoming joint publication. Despite its significance, accurately detecting abnormal airway dilatation has proved difficult in medical imaging studies, especially when bronchial walls become very thin and hard to distinguish from surrounding tissues.  Existing methods based on traditional medical imaging techniques often struggle due to factors like partial volume effects, poor contrast, and air-filled structures that make it hard to differentiate dilatated airways from normal ones.  In order to enhance accuracy in diagnosing abnormal airway dilatation, particularly in young children with cystic fibrosis, this study explored the use of automatic detection based on MRI images.  A dataset containing 126 MRI scans of cystic fibrosis patients was used to develop and evaluate a novel approach combining Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) and semi-supervised techniques.  When training the network with only positively labeled images, it was seen that it could differentiate between normal and abnormally dilated airways with an accuracy of 75.9% when assessing 294 airway segments from the training dataset, and 69.3% when assessing 412 airway segments from the testing dataset.  When using a small set of positively and negatively labeled images for cross-entropy loss and adversarial techniques, it was observed that it could accurately identify both normal and dilatated airways with high precision, especially in situations where only positively labeled data was available.  A model developed using the entire positive training dataset, and another using the combined positive and negative training dataset, was tested and evaluated with unseen data, resulting in improved accuracy of 81.9% and 65.5% respectively when assessing 412 airway segments from the testing dataset.  When assessing entire scans instead of individual airway segments, it was seen that it could accurately identify cystic fibrosis patients with abnormally dilated airways with an accuracy of 90.5% and 83.2% for the two models respectively.  A comparison was made with a traditional U-Net approach, resulting in better performance when assessing individual airway segments and comparable results when assessing entire scans.  This research provides a starting point for exploring the use of MRI images in detecting abnormal airway dilatation, and it is believed that accuracy can be further improved with the use of larger training datasets and more advanced techniques.  In addition, it is anticipated that such a detection method could aid clinical diagnosis and tracking of disease progression by identifying dilatated airways

This research explores the integration of atmosphere and voxel-based scene representation.  It proposes a simple screen-space ambient occlusion technique to handle dark shadows, while a physically based rendering approach is used to handle the high dynamic range lighting found in real-world scenes.  The method also incorporates a technique to remove unwanted dark areas produced by shallow voxel objects, thereby enabling the accurate depiction of illumination in scenes with both bright skies and deep shadows.  The outcomes of this research are showcased through rendered images of various scenes.  The integrated approach has the added benefit of facilitating the inclusion of artificial lighting sources within voxel environments.  The technique is versatile and may be applied to the rendering of both indoor and outdoor scenes, and is compatible with a range of rendering techniques, including global illumination.  The results are presented in the form of rendered images obtained using a custom-made OpenGL application, enabled online for further exploration.
